opening: We often think of prayer as bringing our needs before God, asking for His help, healing, or guidance. But what happens when we don't ask? Does God still recognize what we need?
body:
Today's Gospel tells the story of a woman who had been bent over for eighteen years, unable to stand upright.

What struck me was that she never asked Jesus to heal her.

She was simply present in the synagogue on the Sabbath. I imagine she may have been coming to worship for many years, carrying the burden of her condition, perhaps no longer expecting anything to change.  

Yet Jesus saw her.

He called her forward, declared her free of her infirmity, and laid His hands upon her. Immediately, she stood upright and glorified God.

I find something extraordinarily moving about this encounter. Jesus knew her suffering without her having to explain it. He recognized her need before she expressed it.

And He chose to heal her openly, in the presence of everyone.

Then came the objection.

The synagogue leader, indignant that Jesus had healed on the Sabbath, told the crowd there were six days on which people should come to be cured.

But this woman hadn't come asking to be cured. At least, the Gospel gives us no indication that she had.

She was simply there.

And Jesus, seeing her suffering, acted.

When the leader objected, Jesus called out the hypocrisy. He reminded them that even on the Sabbath, they untied their oxen and donkeys to lead them to water.

Then He asked:

“This daughter of Abraham, whom Satan has bound for eighteen years now, ought she not to have been set free on the sabbath day from this bondage?” — Luke 13:16

I had never considered the comparison quite this way.

The animals were tied, yet their owners understood the need to release them for water. This woman had been bound by her suffering for eighteen years, yet someone questioned whether she should be released because of the day of the week.

They recognized the needs of their animals but struggled to recognize the freedom owed to a daughter of Abraham.

And Jesus called her exactly that.

Not a crippled woman. Not a burden. Not someone whose condition defined her.

A daughter of Abraham.

Her suffering had changed the way she carried herself through the world, but it had never changed who she was in God's eyes.

I also wonder about the deliberate, public nature of this healing. Jesus called her forward and laid His hands upon her where everyone could see. Her restoration became something the entire congregation witnessed.

Perhaps this was more than a physical healing. It was also a revelation of how God sees those whom others may have grown accustomed to overlooking.

In today's first reading, Paul asks us to imitate God and live in love as His beloved children.

What a remarkable example Jesus gives us.

He does not wait for the woman to prove her worthiness, find the right words, or ask at the proper time. He sees her need and responds with compassion.

And perhaps that is something we forget in our own relationship with Him.

We may believe that God knows everything about us, yet still live as though we must explain ourselves before He will understand. We may become so accustomed to carrying our burdens that we no longer imagine anything could change.

But this woman reminds me that God's awareness of us does not begin with our asking.

What I especially love about this Gospel is its joy.

The woman stands upright and glorifies God. The crowd rejoices at the wonderful things Jesus has done.

Reading it nearly two thousand years later, I feel some of that same happiness and relief, as though I have been allowed to witness her freedom myself.

And perhaps that is one of the beautiful gifts of Scripture. We may not have stood in that synagogue, but we can still recognize the goodness of what happened there.

Eighteen years of suffering. One encounter with Christ. And a woman who could finally stand upright.

For eighteen years, her condition determined how she faced the world. But it never determined how Jesus saw her.

Perhaps the miracle is not only that she was healed, but that she was seen, known, and loved before she ever asked.
prayer: Lord Jesus,  Thank You for seeing us even when we do not know how to ask for Your help.  You know the burdens we carry, the suffering we have grown accustomed to, and the needs we cannot always express.  Help us trust that Your love is not limited by our words, our circumstances, or our understanding.  Teach us to recognize the dignity of others, especially those whose suffering we may have stopped noticing.  And when Your goodness reaches someone else's life, may we rejoice rather than question, remembering that Your mercy is never diminished by being shared.  Holy Spirit, open our hearts to recognize Christ's presence and to live as His beloved children.  Amen.
theme: Sometimes God's love reaches us before we even know what to ask for.
title: Thank you for seeing me Jesus
